Body of This Death
BOD-ee uv this DETH
n. phr. (the condition from which Paul cries to be delivered, Romans 7:24)
Greek to sōma tou thanatou toutou — sōma, body, and thanatos, death. The phrase may be read as the body belonging to this death, or as this body of death.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

At the end of his account of the inward war Paul breaks into a cry: “O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” The answer follows at once: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin.” The phrase gathers the whole chapter. It is not a complaint about the physical body as such, which Paul elsewhere calls the temple of the Holy Ghost and expects to be redeemed; it names the whole condition of a man in whom indwelling sin still operates — what he has just described as evil present with him when he would do good. The cry is who, not what: Paul does not ask for a technique but for a deliverer, and the answer is a Person. Reformed exposition has generally taken the speaker to be the regenerate man, and the grammar supports it, for an unconverted man does not delight in the law of God after the inward man. That reading is the pastorally decisive one, because it means this wretchedness is the normal experience of a true Christian and not evidence against his conversion. Thanksgiving and unfinished conflict stand in the same breath. The deliverance is certain and already given in Christ, and the warfare continues until the body itself is redeemed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Body, the frame of an animal; also, the main part or mass of any thing. The body of this death, Romans 7:24, the whole condition of man under indwelling sin, from which deliverance is sought.

Body, the frame or material substance of an animal.

Greek sōma, body; thanatos, death.

O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me, Romans 7:24.

The answer is personal: I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord, Romans 7:25.

Key Scripture

Rom 7:24 — "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?"

Rom 7:25 — "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin."

Rom 7:22 — "For I delight in the law of God after the inward man:"

Rom 8:23 — "And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body."

Modern Corruption

The cry is treated as a stage the mature Christian leaves behind, or else as evidence that Paul was not yet converted, and either way the believer's ordinary experience of indwelling sin is made abnormal.

expand to see more

Perfectionist and higher-life teaching has long read Romans 7 as the condition of a defeated Christian who has not yet entered the victorious life of Romans 8, so that a believer who recognises himself in verse 24 is told he is living below his privileges. The pastoral damage is considerable: sincere Christians conclude that their continuing struggle is a failure of consecration, and they oscillate between pretended victory and private despair. Paul gives no such ladder. Thanksgiving for deliverance and the acknowledgment of serving the law of sin with the flesh stand in the same verse, and Romans 8 itself still groans, waiting for the redemption of the body.

The opposite reading makes the speaker an unregenerate man under conviction, which removes the difficulty by removing Paul. It founders on verse 22, where the speaker delights in the law of God after the inward man — a thing Romans 8:7 says the carnal mind cannot do. The therapeutic culture then adds a third distortion by renaming the whole experience as shame to be resolved rather than sin to be fought, so that the cry becomes a symptom and the deliverer becomes unnecessary. Scripture's own shape should be kept exactly: a real wretchedness, honestly named; a real deliverance, already secured in Christ; and a real conflict that continues until the body is redeemed. The principle to recover is that assurance and struggle are not rivals in the Christian life.
